Q: imap_tools Mailbox.move showing MailboxExpungeError and UID Command Error (Python3) A:

Seems you should use .uids()

There is many examples at docs, this is for your case:

with MailBox('imap.mail.com').login('test@mail.com', 'pwd', initial_folder='INBOX') as mailbox:
    # MOVE all messages from current folder to INBOX/folder2, move by 100 emails at once
    mailbox.move(mailbox.uids(), 'INBOX/folder2', chunks=100)

Regards, lib author

Q: Why does the command prompt appear on a new line after C program execution, even without \n? A:

A since-deleted, putatively AI-generated answer (only users with sufficient reputation can view the link) actually provided good insights; let me provide a 100% human-generated perspective.

There are two distinct, unrelated aspects to consider:

  • (a) Printing external program output to the console (terminal).

  • (b) Capturing such output in a file, using >, i.e. I/O redirection.

Re (a)

By design, both cmd.exe and PowerShell - unlike most POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash[0] - ensure that a newline is always printed following command output before re-printing their prompt string in interactive sessions - even if the external program output does not end in a newline, such as in your case.

Thus, a program printing, say, printf("foo"); produces the same display output as one emitting printf("foo\n");:

Presumably, the design rationale is to ensure that the prompt string always prints at the start of a line, for visual consistency.
There is no way to modify this behavior in PowerShell that I am aware of.[1]

Re (b)

While it is understandable to try to use an I/O redirection, >, to capture an external program's raw byte output, this does not work as intended in Windows PowerShell, the legacy, ships-with-Windows, Windows-only edition of PowerShell whose latest and final version is 5.1:

  • External-program output is invariably first decoded, based on the encoding stored in [Console]::OutputEncoding, ...

  • ... and then re-encoded on saving to the target file, using the default encoding of the Out-File cmdlet, of which > is a virtual alias, and that default encoding happens to be UTF-16 LE (in which ASCII-range characters such as h are represented as 2-byte sequences with the low-order byte representing the ASCII code point and the high-order byte being 0x0, e.g. 68 00 for 'h'), preceded by a BOM (the FF FE by sequence shown at the start of your Format-Hex output).

  • Additionally, the external-program output is decoded line by line, and each line is written to the target file with a trailing newline, using the platform-native newline format, which is CRLF on Windows (\r\n, in printf terms) - whether or not the output's last line had a trailing newline.
    Thus, similarly to the to-console output, a program printing, say, printf("foo"); produces the same file content as one emitting printf("foo\n"); when redirected with >, the redirection operator

  • It is worth noting that even in PowerShell (Core) 7 (see below) the decoding behavior still applies with respect to further processing external-program output in memory, and the re-encoding behavior still applies when using explicit calls to file-saving cmdlets such as Out-File, though PowerShell 7 notably and commendably consistently defaults to BOM-less UTF-8.[2]

  • The simplest way to ensure capturing of raw bytes from external programs in Windows PowerShell is to delegate to cmd.exe, whose > operator does just that:

    # Windows PowerShell:
# Captures raw byte output from .\r.exe 
# Note: \ rather than / must be used for cmd.exe's sake.
cmd /c .\r.exe > output.txt

By contrast, it does work as intended in PowerShell (Core) 7, the modern, cross-platform, install-on-demand edition, in v7.4+ (older versions are now out of support), i.e. > captures raw byte output, the same way it does in cmd.exe and in most POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash.[0]

    # PowerShell (Core) 7.4+:
    # Captures raw byte output from ./r.exe, both on Windows and Unix-like platforms.
    ./r.exe > output.txt

[0] As Charlie Harding points out in a comment on the question, the lone exception among the major POSIX-compatible shells is zsh, which also ensures that a newline is printed, but additionally visually highlights the lack of a trailing newline in program output by following its last line with a % printed in reverse video; the - non-POSIX-compatible - fish shell uses ⏎ instead; see this blog post for details.

[1] By contrast, a hack is available if you use cmd.exe rather than PowerShell, as explained by Neil in a comment on the question: Batch files whose last line contains (just) : suppress the mechanism that implicitly adds a newline to the output from programs not ending in a newline, so you could wrap calls to such programs in such a batch file.

[2] Windows PowerShell is, unfortunately, wildly inconsistent with respect to default character encodings - see the bottom section of this answer.
